content: UnitedHealth Group closed at $341.88 on Tuesday, November 24. That is 21.2% below its highest close of the past year, on July 21, once that close is adjusted for dividends paid since. If the whole market turns, how far could the stock fall, and how long could you wait to get back? Including dividends, the stock lost 12.3% in the week to Tuesday, while the S&P 500 fell 1.9%. The price fell 10.2% on Wednesday, November 18, alone. The fall followed a federal proposal that could let regulators recover Medicare Advantage overpayments dating back to 2018. Medicare Advantage plans are private health plans for seniors. For more on that day, see Why Is UnitedHealth Stock Falling? This fall is not one of the market shocks below. A market shock would come on top of it. Its deepest fall in a market shock came in the 2008-2009 Global Financial Crisis. The stock fell 72% from its close on December 26, 2007, when that shock began. The S&P 500 fell 53% over the same window. Across all 15 shocks since 2007, counting one where it did not fall, the stock fell 17% on average, against 15.8% for the S&P 500. The stock got back to its peak close in 13 of the 14 shocks where it fell. Counting each of those 13 shocks, the median wait was 2.8 months from the lowest close. Only the climb back from the 2008-2009 fall took longer than a year. UnitedHealth needed 40.2 months to climb back after the 2008-2009 fall. If you live off your savings, a wait that long can mean selling shares at low prices to cover your bills. The stock has not got back to its April 11, 2025 close, its peak in the 2025 US Tariff Shock window. On closes adjusted for dividends, it closed Tuesday 40.7% below that close. The gap covers everything since then, including this month’s fall, so the shock is not its only cause. Revenue was $113 billion in the three months to September 30, 2026. That was 0.4% lower than a year earlier. Operating margin, the share of revenue left after running costs, was 5.3% over the four quarters to September 2026. Over the four quarters to September 2023, it was 8.8%. Total debt was $74.3 billion on September 30, 2026. Three years earlier it was $63.4 billion. Medical costs in employer plans are the first risk. On its October 13 call, management said the yearly rise in those costs was running above the 11% it first expected. It said the pressure would “stretch out our ability to achieve those long term objectives and margins” in that business. Medicaid, the state health plans for low-income families, is the second risk. Management called 2026 the low point for core Medicaid margins, which it expected to be “moderately better than negative 1%”. Management also raised its 2026 guide for adjusted earnings per share, which leaves out some one-time items. The new guide is at least $20.50, up from $19.75 in the previous release. The cost warnings and the higher guide point different ways. Management said it would give a fuller outlook for next year before year-end.
